# 1 Maccabees Chapter 6 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 6

---

## Council Notes

**On the death of Antiochus IV (vv.8-16):** This is the chapter's theological centerpiece. The dying king's confession (vv.10-13) is remarkable — he attributes his fate directly to his despoliation of Jerusalem and the Torah. The author presents Antiochus's own deathbed self-understanding as confirmatory of divine judgment. The passage should be translated with gravity.

**On the elephant warfare (vv.30-47):** The extended description of the Seleucid war elephants is one of the most vivid battle descriptions in the Deuterocanon. The detail about showing them red grape juice to excite them, the wooden towers, the Indian mahouts — these are historically credible details. The battle of Beth-zechariah (162 BCE) is independently corroborated by Josephus.

**On Eleazar Avaran (vv.43-46):** This is among the most dramatic individual acts of the book. The author records Eleazar's death as a deliberate self-sacrifice (*edoken heauton*) for the sake of his people and everlasting name. The irony — that he killed the wrong elephant, not the king — is unstated but present. The narrative presents his act as heroic regardless of outcome.

**On "juice of grapes and mulberries" (v.34):** EMET preserves "juice of grapes and mulberries." LOGOS: "blood of grapes and mulberries" — the Greek *haima* here is literally "blood" (in the sense of "sap/juice"); the red color was intended to excite the animals. "Juice" is clearer in English.

**On the broken oath (v.62):** The king breaks his sworn terms the moment he sees the strength of the position. This is a standard theme in the book: Seleucid promises cannot be trusted. The narrative records it without editorial comment — the fact speaks for itself.

---

1. King Antiochus was moving through the upper provinces when he heard that in Persia there was a city called Elymais, renowned for its wealth in silver and gold.
2. Its temple was very rich, containing golden shields, breastplates, and weapons that Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian, who first reigned over the Greeks, had left there.
3. He came to try to take the city and plunder it, but he could not, because his plan became known to the people of the city,
4. and they rose up against him in battle. He fled and departed in great distress, to return to Babylon.
5. A messenger came to him in Persia reporting that the armies sent into Judah had been defeated:
6. that Lysias had advanced with a strong force but had been driven back before the Judeans; that the Judeans had grown strong in arms and forces and with abundant plunder from the armies they had cut down;
7. that they had demolished the abomination he had erected on the altar in Jerusalem, that they had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and had also fortified Beth-zur, one of his cities.
8. When the king heard this, he was astonished and deeply shaken. He lay down on his bed and fell into illness from grief, because things had not turned out as he had planned.
9. He remained there many days, for great grief kept returning upon him, and he knew that he was dying.
10. He called all his Friends and said to them: "Sleep has departed from my eyes, and my heart is weighed down with worry.
11. I said to myself: 'Into what great tribulation have I come, and into what a flood of misery I am now sunk — I who was kind and beloved in my power!'
12. But now I remember the wrongs I did in Jerusalem — how I took away all the gold and silver vessels there, and sent to destroy the inhabitants of Judah for no reason.
13. I know it is because of this that these evils have overtaken me; and see — I am dying in bitter grief in a foreign land."
14. He called Philip, one of his Friends, and appointed him over his entire kingdom.
15. He gave him his diadem, his robe, and his signet ring, with instructions to raise his son Antiochus and to bring him to power as king.
16. King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year.
17. When Lysias learned that the king was dead, he installed the king's young son Antiochus in his place — the boy he had been raising — and named him Eupator.
18. Meanwhile the garrison of the citadel was blockading Israel around the sanctuary, constantly seeking to harm them and to strengthen the Gentile cause.
19. Judas resolved to destroy them, and assembled all the people to lay siege to them.
20. They gathered and laid siege in the one hundred and fiftieth year; he built siege-towers and war machines against them.
21. But some of those besieged in the citadel escaped, and certain renegades of Israel joined them
22. and went to the king, saying: "How long will you fail to act and do justice for our cause?
23. We were willing to serve your father, to live by his decrees and to follow his orders.
24. For this our own countrymen have been besieging us; and they have killed everyone of us they could seize, and plundered our estates.
25. Not only against us have they stretched out their hand, but against all our borders.
26. Even now they are encamped against the citadel in Jerusalem to take it; and they have fortified the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
27. If you do not act against them quickly, they will go even further, and you will not be able to stop them."
28. When the king heard this, he was enraged. He assembled all his Friends, the commanders of his infantry, and the officers of the cavalry.
29. Mercenary forces came to him from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.
30. The total of his forces was one hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for battle.
31. They came through Idumea and encamped before Beth-zur. They attacked it over many days and built siege engines; but the garrison sallied out and burned them and fought courageously.
32. Judas withdrew from the citadel and moved to Beth-zechariah, opposite the camp of the king.
33. The king rose early and moved his army swiftly along the road to Beth-zechariah. The armies took battle formation and sounded the trumpets.
34. They showed the elephants the juice of grapes and mulberries, to excite them for battle.
35. The animals were distributed among the phalanxes; with each elephant a thousand men armed with coats of mail and bronze helmets were stationed, and five hundred chosen cavalry were assigned to each beast.
36. These were ready wherever the beast was; wherever it went they went with it and never left its side.
37. On the elephants were wooden towers of strength, covered and firmly fastened to each with special harness; on each were four fighting men who fought from above, and also an Indian mahout.
38. The remaining cavalry was placed on both flanks of the army, to harass the enemy and to be protected within the infantry units.
39. When the sun shone on the golden and bronze shields, the mountains gleamed with them and blazed like torches of fire.
40. Part of the king's army spread out over the high ground, and part over the lower ground; they advanced confidently and in formation.
41. All the inhabitants of the land were shaken by the sound of their multitude, the tramping of the companies, and the clash of weapons — for it was a very great and powerful army.
42. Judas and his army advanced to engage, and six hundred men from the king's army fell.
43. Eleazar, called Avaran, saw that one of the elephants was fitted with royal armor and was taller than all the rest; he assumed the king was riding on it,
44. and he gave himself up to save his people and to win for himself an everlasting name.
45. He ran boldly at it through the midst of the phalanx, cutting down men on his right and left; they parted before him on both sides.
46. He got in underneath the elephant, drove his blade up into it from below, and killed it; the elephant fell to the earth upon him, and he died there.
47. But when the Judeans saw the strength of the royal army and the fury of its assault, they drew back from it.
48. The king's forces advanced toward Jerusalem; the army encamped in Judea and before Mount Zion.
49. He made peace with the people of Beth-zur; they came out of the city, for they had no food to sustain a prolonged siege, since it was a sabbatical year for the land.
50. The king took Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to hold it.
51. He then encamped before the sanctuary for many days, setting up there war machines — catapults, fire-throwers, stone-hurlers, arrow-launchers, and slings.
52. The defenders also built machines to counter the attackers'; the siege continued for many days.
53. But there were no provisions in the storerooms, because it was the seventh year, and the refugees who had fled to Judea from the Gentiles had consumed whatever remained of the stores.
54. Only a few men were left in the sanctuary; hunger had overcome the rest and they had scattered to their homes.
55. Then Lysias heard that Philip — whom King Antiochus while still alive had appointed to raise his son Antiochus as king —
56. had returned from Persia and Media with the forces that had accompanied the king, and was now trying to seize control of the government.
57. In his urgency to withdraw, he said to the king, the commanders, and the troops: "We grow weaker every day; our provisions are scarce; the place we are besieging is strong; and the affairs of the kingdom demand our attention.
58. Let us therefore offer terms to these men, make peace with them and with their whole nation,
59. and allow them to live according to their own customs as before — for it was our abolishing their customs that provoked them to anger and to all these actions."
60. The proposal pleased the king and the commanders, and he sent them an offer of peace, which they accepted.
61. The king and the commanders swore to them on all these terms; they came out of the stronghold.
62. The king entered Mount Zion. When he saw how strong the position was, he broke the oath he had sworn and ordered the wall all around it to be demolished.
63. He then left in haste and returned to Antioch, where he found Philip already in control of the city. He fought against him and took the city by force.
